references.text: Isaiah prophesies that God's house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples. Jesus quotes this verse (in the broader context with parallels from Mark and Matthew) when he drives out the merchants from the temple: "my house shall be called a house of prayer" ([ref:Jes 56:7|Isaiah 56:7]).

Jeremiah accuses the people of having made the Lord's house a "den of robbers". Jesus uses exactly this expression in connection with the cleansing of the temple, as shown by the parallel passages ([ref:Jer 7:11|Jeremiah 7:11]).

Matthew's parallel account of Jesus' cleansing of the temple, where he drives out those who were buying and selling, overturns the tables of the money changers, and quotes Isaiah and Jeremiah ([ref:Matt 21:12-13|Matthew 21:12-13]).

Mark's parallel account of the cleansing of the temple, with a more detailed description of how Jesus drove out the buyers and sellers, overturned the tables of the money changers, and emphasized that the temple should be a house of prayer ([ref:Mark 11:15-17|Mark 11:15-17]).

John's account of Jesus' cleansing of the temple, placed early in his ministry, where he makes a whip and drives out those who were selling oxen, sheep, and doves, and overturns the tables of the money changers ([ref:Joh 2:14-16|John 2:14-16]).

Malachi prophesies that the Lord will suddenly come to his temple and cleanse the sons of Levi. Jesus' cleansing of the temple can be seen as a fulfillment of this prophecy about the Lord's sudden coming to purify his own house ([ref:Mal 3:1-3|Malachi 3:1-3]).

Zechariah prophesies that on that day there shall no longer be any Canaanite (merchant) in the house of the Lord, the God of hosts. Jesus' action of driving out the sellers from the temple points toward the fulfillment of this prophecy ([ref:Sak 14:21|Zechariah 14:21]).
